title: Decisions Are Processes, Not Events
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that decision quality is decided long before the moment of choice, in how the problem is framed, tested and shared. Drawing on her consulting work, she offers three principles she wishes she had learned earlier. The first is that reframing a question changes the options a leader can see, illustrated by an interview project derailed by an opaque technical term. The second is that good decision-makers test their thinking rather than defend it, treating decisions as working hypotheses. The third is that people commit faster to decisions they helped shape, which she illustrates with a co-creation strategy process for the UK Data Service. The closing move recasts decision-making as a collaborative, iterative process that builds trust and speed. The post ends with a pitch for a subscriber-only decisions field guide.
points: Framing the problem is where most decisions are won or lost, so changing the language of a question can surface options that were invisible before.
Defence mode optimises for being right while testing mode optimises for getting it right, so leaders should expose ideas to stress-testing by those who must implement them.
Co-creation workshops across levels of seniority produce ownership, whereas decisions delivered to people tend to meet slow uptake or surface compliance.
A fragile idea that collapses under challenge is a useful discovery, not a failure of the challenger.
quotes: Most poor decisions don’t fail at the moment you actually make a choice. They fail much earlier, at the moment the problem you’re trying to solve is framed.

I went back to the client and proposed a full reframe: simpler language, clearer prompts and an entry point that people could actually relate to. Once we did that, the quality of insight changed dramatically.

The realisation was that defence mode optimises for being right, whereas testing mode optimises for getting it right. So, great decision-makers expose their ideas rather than defending them. They treat decisions like working hypotheses, not finished arguments.
Testing your thinking is not a sign of uncertainty, but a discipline. It helps you avoid blind spots and strengthen your decisions before they meet reality.

Even the best decisions fail to materialise if the people responsible for acting on them don’t feel any ownership. You can have perfect logic and a beautifully structured plan, but if the decision is delivered to people rather than built with them, the reaction is predictable: you will likely experience slow uptake or only surface compliance.

Decision-making is rarely about finding the one perfect choice (often, there isn’t one!). In most cases, it’s about expertly shaping how you and others are thinking, so you can make informed, shared decisions with the other people in the room.
